title: Individual Autonomy and the Ethics of Euthanasia
text: Individual autonomy provides the strongest ethical justification for euthanasia. In my view, mentally competent individuals should retain the right to make decisions about their own lives, particularly when they are facing terminal illnesses that offer no realistic possibility of recovery. This principle is not controversial in most areas of medicine. Patients are already allowed to refuse surgeries, medications, and life-sustaining treatments, even when doing so may shorten their lives. For that reason, denying patients the option of euthanasia appears ethically inconsistent. If individuals are trusted to make significant medical decisions throughout their lives, they should also be trusted to make decisions at the end of life. My perspective on this issue was shaped during high school, when I watched several interviews with terminally ill patients while researching medical ethics for a class project. What struck me was not simply their physical pain, but it was their desire to maintain control over their remaining time and dignity. Many of them understood that death was inevitable and their concern was how they would spend their final weeks or months. Some feared becoming entirely dependent on others, while others wished to avoid prolonged suffering that offered no possibility of improvement. These accounts convinced me that autonomy is not merely an abstract philosophical concept, but it directly affects the quality of a person's final experiences. Furthermore, evidence from countries that have legalized euthanasia under strict regulations suggests that individual choice can coexist with legal safeguards. Requirements such as psychological evaluations, informed consent, and multiple medical assessments help prevent abuse while preserving personal freedom. Therefore, when implemented within a carefully regulated framework, euthanasia respects a fundamental ethical principle: the right of individuals to determine the course of their own lives, even at its end.

title: Authenticity Against Social Performance
text: The truck driver represents authentic resistance to a society built on performative validation. While most characters in the episode are deeply invested in maintaining high social ratings, she stands out as someone who has consciously detached herself from that system, making her one of the most symbolically important figures in Lacie’s journey. She functions as a direct contrast to Lacie, whose entire identity is shaped by external approval. From the beginning of the episode, Lacie carefully performs an idealized version of herself in order to gain positive ratings and improve her social status. She rehearses her smiles in the mirror, adjusts her tone of voice to sound more pleasant, and even stages small everyday moments, such as taking a carefully arranged photo of a cookie and coffee to appear desirable online. These details reveal that her life is not guided by authentic self-expression, but by strategic self-presentation. The truck driver, however, exists outside this culture of performance. Her lower social rating has already excluded her from practical privileges, such as access to better transportation options. Yet unlike Lacie, whose declining score leads to desperation and emotional instability, the truck driver appears psychologically freer rather than defeated. She does not perform the exaggerated politeness expected in this society or carefully manage her personality for approval. Instead, she speaks bluntly, openly expresses frustration, and shows little concern for how others perceive her. Her story about losing her husband adds significant emotional depth because it reveals the human cost of a culture that suppresses authentic emotion. After his death, she stopped pretending to be endlessly pleasant simply to satisfy strangers’ expectations, suggesting that profound grief made the social rating system feel trivial and absurd. This moment is especially important because it exposes the incompatibility between real human suffering and a culture built on performative positivity. In a world where emotional control is constantly rewarded, grief becomes a social disadvantage rather than a natural human response. Through her interaction with Lacie, the truck driver symbolizes an authentic form of identity grounded in lived experience rather than social approval.

title: The Stress of Rush Hour Bus Commutes
text: Rush hour bus commutes are one of the most frustrating parts of my daily life. Looking at this picture immediately reminds me of mornings when I stand in a long, unmoving line with my backpack on, checking the time every few seconds. Everyone around me looks half-awake, tired, and impatient, yet the atmosphere stays strangely silent except for the sound of traffic and the bus engine. What drives me insane is that feeling of helplessness. I might wake up early, skip breakfast to save time, and rush out of the house thinking I planned everything perfectly, only to end up stuck in a situation like this. The worst moment is when the bus finally arrives and people suddenly start moving forward faster, creating that small wave of urgency, as if everyone is silently competing for a spot. For one second, I feel relieved, but that disappears the moment I see how packed the inside already is. If I manage to get on, I am squeezed between strangers, barely able to breathe comfortably, trying to keep my balance every time the bus jerks forward or stops suddenly. Sometimes someone’s bag keeps hitting my arm, or I am forced to stand in an awkward position for the entire ride. If I cannot get on at all, the frustration is even worse because I know waiting for the next bus means being even later. Situations like this do not just annoy me, but they mentally drain me before my day has even properly started.

title: Stillness Painted in Bold Colors
text: One of the most striking features of this painting is its powerful use of color as an emotional and expressive technique. Rather than using realistic skin tones, shadows, or natural environmental colors, the artist deliberately chooses bold, unnatural colors to create mood and visual impact. The bright red chair immediately dominates the composition, drawing the viewer’s eye toward the center of the painting and creating a sense of warmth, energy, and emotional intensity. Red is often associated with passion, vitality, or strong emotion, yet in this context, it contrasts interestingly with the calm posture of the sleeping woman, creating a balance between energy and tranquility. In contrast, the woman’s body is painted with pale white and soft bluish tones, giving her an almost dreamlike, delicate appearance. The cool tones make her seem peaceful, fragile, and distant, which strengthens the impression of quiet rest or introspection. The background also plays an important role, featuring warm orange, brown, and green decorative patterns that add richness and texture without overwhelming the central figure. This layering of warm and cool colors demonstrates the artist’s intentional contrast technique, where opposing color temperatures are used to create visual tension and harmony at the same time. Instead of blending colors smoothly to imitate realism, the artist applies them in large, flat areas with clear boundaries, a technique commonly associated with modernist painting and influenced by Fauvism, where emotional expression becomes more important than accurate representation. Because of this, viewers do not simply observe the painting as a realistic portrait but experience it emotionally through its color relationships.

title: How to Drive Your Teacher Crazy
text: If someone wants to drive a teacher crazy, the process is surprisingly simple. First, arrive late to class as often as possible and make sure to enter the room loudly. Open the door slowly, drop your bag on the floor, and greet your friends while everyone is trying to work. This immediately interrupts the lesson and distracts the entire class. Next, ask questions about directions that were already explained in detail. For example, after the teacher spends ten minutes discussing homework, raise your hand and ask what assignment is due tomorrow. Another effective method is to forget important materials such as pencils, notebooks, paper, or textbooks. Then, spend several minutes asking classmates if you can borrow their supplies. Similarly, you can also talk while the teacher is speaking, especially about topics that have nothing to do with class. Laughing with friends during serious moments can make the situation even worse. It is also helpful to complain constantly about homework, quizzes, projects, grades, or deadlines, even when they are fair. Furthermore, when the teacher asks for volunteers or class participation, remain completely silent and avoid eye contact. However, the moment the bell rings, suddenly become loud, energetic, and ready to socialize. By combining lateness, interruptions, and constant complaints, anyone could successfully drive a teacher crazy in a short amount of time.

title: Teaching Beyond Code
text: A computer science teacher is an appealing profession because effective teaching can transform how students understand complex concepts. My interest in this field stems largely from my experience taking the IB Computer Science course during high school, where I was first introduced to structured programming, algorithmic thinking, and the broader logic underlying computational systems. While the course itself was intellectually stimulating, what left a more lasting impression on me was the role of the teacher in guiding students through abstract concepts that initially seemed inaccessible. For instance, when I struggled to understand recursion and data structures, my teacher employed step-by-step visualizations and real-world analogies. This transformed what felt like an overwhelming topic into something both manageable and engaging. This experience made me realize that effective teaching in computer science is not merely about delivering content, but about facilitating a shift in perspective; helping students develop a problem-solving mindset that extends beyond the classroom. Moreover, through collaborative projects such as designing a simple database system, I experienced firsthand how guidance and feedback can significantly enhance both technical proficiency and confidence. These experiences have led me to value the pedagogical aspect of computer science as much as the discipline itself. It also motivated me to pursue a career where I can contribute to making complex concepts accessible and inspiring for future learners.

title: Diving into Profession: Deep-Sea Fisherman
text: Deep-sea fishermen must possess resilience, technical expertise, and adaptability in order to operate effectively in one of the most demanding professions in the world. To begin with, resilience is indispensable, as these individuals are required to endure prolonged periods of physical and psychological strain. They frequently remain at sea for weeks at a time, performing extended shifts with minimal rest, thereby necessitating exceptional stamina. Furthermore, they must continue their work under severe environmental conditions, including storms and extreme cold, without compromising operational efficiency. Secondly, technical expertise is a defining characteristic of a competent deep-sea fisherman, given the complexity of the tasks involved. For example, fishermen must possess a thorough understanding of navigation systems and oceanographic patterns to identify productive fishing zones. Additionally, they are responsible for operating sophisticated machinery, such as trawling equipment and winches, where even minor errors may result in equipment malfunction or significant injury. Lastly, adaptability is essential due to the inherently unpredictable nature of the marine environment. Fishermen must promptly modify their strategies in response to fluctuations in fish populations or unforeseen mechanical issues. Similarly, they must react effectively to sudden environmental changes, including shifting currents, to maintain both safety and productivity. In conclusion, resilience, technical expertise, and adaptability collectively constitute the foundational qualities of a proficient deep-sea fisherman, enabling them to navigate the multifaceted challenges intrinsic to their profession.

title: The Emotional Burden of Teaching
text: One of the greatest challenges of teaching is the emotional responsibility that extends beyond the classroom. Teachers are expected not only to educate students but also to recognize when something is wrong in their personal lives. For example, a student who used to participate actively in class may suddenly become quiet and stop completing assignments. At first, the teacher might assume that the student has simply lost interest in school. However, as the behavior continues, the teacher may begin to suspect that the student is dealing with problems at home or difficulties with friends. This puts the teacher in an uncomfortable position. Ignoring the situation feels irresponsible, but asking too many questions could make the student feel pressured or embarrassed. Even if the teacher approaches the student privately, there is no guarantee that the student will open up. Meanwhile, the teacher must continue managing the classroom and giving other students the attention they deserve. What makes this situation especially frustrating and overwhelming is that teachers often have little control over the problems affecting their students. They can listen, offer encouragement, or recommend counseling, but they cannot necessarily change what happens outside school. When a student continues to struggle despite these efforts, teachers may wonder whether they could have done more. Such concerns can remain long after the school day ends, making it difficult to separate work from personal life. Ultimately, one of the hardest parts of teaching is feeling responsible for students' well-being while knowing that some of their problems are beyond a teacher's ability to solve.

title: The Cost of Convenience
text: Technology should remain a tool for human judgment, not a substitute for it. Its ability to simplify difficult tasks and provide immediate access to information has become indispensable in my daily life, particularly as technology becomes capable of handling tasks that once required more effort. Still, I have become increasingly aware of how easily convenience can discourage people from making even simple judgments for themselves. I experienced this one evening when I was meeting a friend near Hongdae. I was already running late, so I entered the restaurant into a navigation app and followed the route without paying much attention to my surroundings. The app directed me to get off at Hongik University Station and walk for about fifteen minutes through several smaller streets. Halfway there, I noticed that another subway station was only a few minutes from the restaurant. Had I checked the map myself instead of immediately following the recommended route, I could have transferred one more stop and avoided most of the walk. The mistake itself was minor, but my reaction bothered me more than the wasted time. I had stopped evaluating the route simply because the app had presented one with confidence and precision. Nothing had prevented me from looking at the surrounding map or considering another option; I had simply treated the recommendation as a decision already made. Since then, I have tried to use navigation differently, checking the overall route before following each instruction automatically. The experience also changed how I think about technology more broadly. Convenience is valuable precisely because it reduces unnecessary effort, but that benefit becomes questionable when it also removes the habit of paying attention and making decisions independently. Technology can guide a decision remarkably well, but deciding whether that guidance makes sense should remain a human responsibility.

title: Beyond the Rules
text: Reading cultivates a sense of language that rules alone cannot explain. A sentence can be grammatically flawless and still feel subtly foreign. An expression may be perfectly correct yet too formal for its register, while a word may satisfy its dictionary definition yet feel misplaced in context. These minor distinctions often separate English that is merely correct from English that feels entirely natural. I notice this most when choosing between words that seem interchangeable at first. Synonyms rarely function as true substitutes. Consider "big" and "substantial": both can describe the same increase, yet "a substantial raise" carries a formality that "a big raise" does not. The difference is easy to recognize but hard to reduce to a rule, since each synonym accumulates its own collocations and expectations through repeated use. A dictionary can catalogue these differences, but it cannot reproduce the thousands of encounters through which they become intuitive. Reading does that, usually without drawing attention to the process. By encountering the same words across different contexts, a reader gradually learns not only what they mean, but where they sound natural and what tone they carry. Over time, this repeated exposure cultivates instinct rather than rule: an awareness of which words habitually appear together. Through reading, I have gradually developed this instinct in my own writing. I may replace a word that is technically correct when it feels unnatural in context, or remove an explanation when the surrounding sentences already make the point clear. These choices often come from patterns I have encountered repeatedly in reading rather than from any specific rule I can identify. None of these revisions makes the writing more grammatical; they make it more deliberate. Rules are better at identifying errors than at negotiating these finer questions of nuance. Thus, extensive reading gradually closes that gap, until choices that once required careful judgment begin to feel instinctive.

title: When Trust Becomes Self-Deception
text: “The Scorpion and the Frog” reveals how easily trust becomes self-deception when clear warnings are dismissed. The fable is simple: a scorpion asks a frog to carry him across a river, promising not to sting because doing so would drown them both. The frog accepts his logic, but halfway across, the scorpion stings him anyway and explains, as they both sink, that it is simply in his nature. The obvious lesson is that some creatures cannot escape what they are, yet the frog's decision seems more revealing than the scorpion's betrayal. He does not trust the scorpion out of ignorance; he trusts him despite knowing exactly what he is. His failure lies in allowing a persuasive argument to outweigh evidence already available to him. That mistake feels uncomfortably familiar. In my own relationships, I have sometimes recognized patterns of unreliability, such as repeated broken promises or a lack of consideration, and still treated them as temporary exceptions rather than evidence of character. The problem was not that the signs were invisible, but that accepting them would have required me to abandon the version of the person I preferred to believe in. Trust becomes dangerous at precisely that point: when it stops responding to evidence and begins protecting an expectation, allowing what we hope someone will become to matter more than what their actions actually show. This does not mean that people are incapable of change, but change must be demonstrated before it can reasonably be trusted. The river therefore represents a boundary between understanding and judgment, the moment when what we know about someone must begin to influence what we are willing to risk for them. The lesson is not to fear every scorpion we meet, but to recognize when faith in another person has become an excuse to distrust our own judgment.

title: Life of Pi: Preserving Meaning in the Void
text: Pi Patel strongly influenced the way I understand resilience. He's the boy in Yann Martel's Life of Pi who, after losing his family in a shipwreck on their way to Canada, finds himself adrift in the Pacific with nothing but a lifeboat, a few tins of biscuits, and a full-grown Bengal tiger. It’s an absurd enough premise that I almost put the book down in the first fifty pages. But what got me wasn't the scale of what he survives; it's what he does with the hours in between surviving. He prays on a schedule. He marks out sections of the lifeboat like they're rooms in a house, this half for me, that half for Richard Parker, and enforces the line as if a tiger cares about property. None of it does anything to the ocean. The water doesn't get calmer because Pi said his prayers that morning, and nothing about his odds of rescue improves because he has drawn a line on a boat. He knows this. And he does it anyway. That's the part I couldn't shake. The rituals aren't there to change his circumstances; they're there to keep those circumstances from becoming the sole author of who he is. Before Pi, I would have said resilience meant your body doesn't quit. But physical survival is a remarkably low bar for what it means to remain intact. Fear and isolation can strip away the routines, convictions, and sense of self by which a person recognizes his own life. It means that you can wash up on a beach very much alive and still bear little resemblance to the person who first set out to sea. But Pi never did. What kept him whole wasn't stamina. It was the fact that he kept deciding, every day, what his suffering was allowed to mean. I don't think I'd have put it this way at fourteen, but I'd put it this way now: staying alive and staying yourself are two different jobs, and the latter is harder.
